newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Caller warns of Hong Kong subway gas attack - police.
newsitem.headline: Caller warns of Hong Kong subway gas attack - police.

text.p: Hong Kong authorities have been placed on a high alert after police received a telephone call threatening a gas attack on the territory's MTR underground train network, the Security Branch said on Monday.
"We received the call on Friday. The call said they would launch a gas attack on the MTR," Branch spokesman Mak Kwok-wah told Reuters after an inquiry about a newspaper report on the threat.

"We have notified various government departments. They are on high alert. But there is no cause for alarm. It may turn out to be false. Anyone can pick up the phone to make the call," Mak said. He said police had adequate resources and capabilities to deal with any situation.
An informed government source told Reuters the caller, speaking Mandarin Chinese, said the attack would be staged on Tuesday night. Mak declined to give further details.

Mak also would not say whether the threat was related to a simmering dispute over rival Japanese and Chinese sovereignty claims to a group of East China Sea islands which has fuelled protests among Chinese communities in Asia in recent months.
But the report in Hong Kong's mass-circulation Chinese-language Apple Daily newspaper linked the threat to Japan's Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth) sect.

"The police received three telephone calls last Friday claiming to be from Japan's Aum Shinry Kyo sect, threatening to release sarin poison gas in carriages on the Hong Kong-Kowloon underground railway tomorrow (Tuesday) evening to get revenge against Hong Kong and Taiwan people who stormed ashore on the Diaoyu islands and planted the flags of China and Taiwan," Apple Daily said.
The sect is accused of being behind a series of sarin nerve gas attacks on the Tokyo subway in 1995 which killed 11 people and injured about 5,500.

The newspaper also said the threat was to take revenge against Hong Kong and Taiwan protesters who landed on the disputed islands, called the Diaoyus by China and the Senkakus by Japan, and raised the Chinese flag there last week.
A spokeswoman for the MTR service declined to give details on precautions being taken after the subway threat but she said police would take charge of special arrangements.
